title: Every Woman Who Walks with a Languid Sway
intro: Al-Mutanabbi slipped out of Egypt at the end of 350 AH (962 CE), escaping its ruler Kafur, and crossed the desert to Iraq; al-Wahidi says he composed this poem on reaching Kufa in Rabi' al-Awwal 351 AH (962 CE). It opens by ranking fast camels above graceful women, then names the stages of the crossing one by one until the camels kneel at Kufa, turns to pride in his loyalty and defiance, mocks Kafur, and closes on the man who does not know his own worth. The modern critic Shawqi Dayf says the poet “packs it with rare words”, and many of them are the names of desert wells and wastes. This recording leaves out nine lines of open mockery of Kafur that come before the last, among them “What laughable things there are in Egypt, but the laughter is like weeping.”

translation: Every woman who walks the slow, swaying walk
is ransom for every camel that walks the fast one,
1.sharh: He would give any woman with a languid, swaying walk in exchange for a fast camel. Poets usually open with love; he opens with his mounts, because he is a traveller, not a lover. Some take the quick pace to be a horse's.

translation: and for every swift camel of Bajawa
that flings out her forefeet; a graceful walk is nothing to me,
2.sharh: The ransom covers every swift Bajawi camel with her lively, outflung stride. A graceful walk means nothing to him, a woman's least of all; what he wants from these camels, the next line says.

translation: but they are the ropes of life,
the means to outwit enemies and push harm away.
3.sharh: The camels are what keep a man alive: they carry him out of danger, let him outwit his enemies and get away from harm. He calls them ropes because he holds on to them to survive.

translation: With them I struck into al-Tih as a gambler casts his lots,
for this or for that.
4.sharh: He rode into al-Tih, the wilderness of Sinai, staking his life like a gambler throwing lots: either he would win and escape, or die and be done with it. “This” and “that” are escape and death.

translation: When they took fright, the horses went before them,
and white swords and brown spears.
5.sharh: They rode the camels and led the horses beside them; when danger came, the horsemen rode ahead with swords and spears to protect them. Al-Ukbari admired the pairing of white swords with brown spears.

translation: They passed by Nakhl, and those who rode them
needed nothing from the world, or from Nakhl.
6.sharh: Nakhl was a known watering place, but they did not stop: they needed neither its water nor anyone's protection, so sure were they of their endurance and their weapons.

translation: By evening at al-Naqab they were offering us a choice:
Wadi al-Miyah or Wadi al-Qura.
7.sharh: At al-Naqab the road forks, and the camels seemed to offer a choice. It was the riders who weighed the two roads; the poet gives the choice to the camels, as poets make camels complain of long night marches.

translation: We asked them, “Where is the land of Iraq?”
and they said, as we stood at Turban, “Here.”
8.sharh: They asked the camels where Iraq was, and the camels answered “Here.” Ibn Jinni says Turban is already in Iraq; others say it is far from it, and the camels are so fast that the distance left is nothing to them.

translation: At Hisma they sprang away as the west wind blows,
heading into the quarter of the east wind,
9.sharh: From Hisma the camels sped like the west wind, heading into the quarter the east wind comes from: from Egypt in the west to Iraq in the east. The verb for a wind blowing also means a camel's eager start.

translation: making for al-Kifaf and Kibd al-Wihad
and al-Buwayra's neighbour, Wadi al-Ghada,
10.sharh: The camels make for these places one after another. The line is a string of names, and that is part of its effect: a desert crossing told stage by stage, as fast as the camels ran it.

translation: They cut through Busayta as a cloak is cut,
between the ostriches and the wild cows,
11.sharh: They crossed Busayta as a blade cuts a cloak from end to end. It is empty land, far from people, where ostriches and wild cows roam without fear, and the camels ran on among them.

translation: on to Uqdat al-Jawf, until they eased
some of their thirst at the water of al-Jurawi.
12.sharh: They reached Uqdat al-Jawf and the water of al-Jurawi, which eased only part of their thirst. Another poet had said that al-Jurawi's water did not cure his thirst, though it slaked the camels'.

translation: Sawar came into sight with the dawn,
and al-Shughur with the late morning.
13.sharh: Sawar came into view at dawn and al-Shughur by late morning. Reaching al-Shughur meant reaching the edge of Iraq, so the long escape was nearly over. The line keeps time as well as place: dawn at one water, mid-morning at the next.

translation: Their swift trot brought them to al-Jumay'i by evening,
and on to al-Adari' at dawn, then al-Dana.
14.sharh: The camels' fast trot carried them to al-Jumay'i by nightfall and on to al-Adari' and al-Dana by morning. The trot itself is made the traveller: they kept it up all night.

translation: What a night it was over A'kush,
black over the land, its waymarks hidden.
15.sharh: He marvels at the night they spent crossing A'kush, so dark that the whole land was black and the stone markers that guide travellers could not be seen, and still they kept going.

translation: We reached al-Ruhayma in the middle of it,
with more of it still to come than had gone.
16.sharh: They reached al-Ruhayma in the middle of the night, with most of it still ahead. Critics asked how most of a night can remain at its middle; Ibn Furraja answered that “its middle” is the middle of A'kush, and al-Wahidi agrees.

translation: When we couched the camels, we planted our spears
on top of our noble deeds and our high rank.
17.sharh: At Kufa they couched the camels and planted their spears in the ground, as travellers do when a journey ends. The spears stood on their honour: the escape and the fights on the road had proved it.

translation: We spent the night kissing our swords
and wiping enemies' blood from them,
18.sharh: That night they kissed their swords, which had brought them out alive, and wiped from them the blood of the men who had fought them on the way.

translation: so that Egypt, and those in Iraq,
and those in al-Awasim, know that I am the man,
19.sharh: All this was so that Egypt, Iraq and al-Awasim would know him for the man he is. Egypt is the country he fled, Iraq his homeland, al-Awasim the realm of his old patron Sayf al-Dawla.

translation: that I kept faith and that I refused,
and that I was overbearing to the overbearing.
20.sharh: Let them know he kept his word, refused to be humiliated, and met arrogance with arrogance. Al-Wahidi takes the faith he kept to be with Sayf al-Dawla; al-Barquqi, his vow to leave Egypt in spite of Kafur.

translation: Not everyone who gives his word keeps it,
nor does everyone made to bear disgrace refuse it.
21.sharh: Not everyone keeps his word, and not everyone refuses when humiliation is forced on him; he did both. The line turns his boast in the line before into a general truth.

translation: The heart must have its instrument,
and judgement that splits solid rock.
22.sharh: Courage is not enough on its own: the heart needs its instrument, which al-Wahidi takes to be reason and good character, and a judgement strong enough to split rock.

translation: Whoever has a heart like mine
cuts through the heart of ruin to reach glory.
23.sharh: A man with a heart like his drives through ruin itself to reach glory. Giving ruin a heart sets it against his own, so that his heart splits the heart of ruin; al-Ukbari praised the figure.

translation: On every road a man takes,
his steps match the length of his leg.
24.sharh: Everyone strides according to the length of his legs: a man achieves in proportion to his capacity. Al-Wahidi calls it a proverb and compares the poet's own “Resolutions come in the measure of the resolute.”

translation: The little servant slept through our night,
as he had slept before: blind, not drowsy.
25.sharh: Kafur, mocked as “the little servant”, slept through the night of their escape, and had been asleep before it, not drowsy but blind to what was being planned around him.

translation: Close as we were to him, there lay between us
deserts of his ignorance and blindness.
26.sharh: Though they lived close by him, his ignorance put deserts between them: he never understood the man at his court. An ignorant man learns nothing from being near.

translation: Whoever is ignorant of his own worth,
others see in him what he cannot see.
27.sharh: A man who does not know his own worth admires himself and is seen through by everyone else: others see the faults he cannot. It closes the attack on Kafur, and al-Barquqi calls it the heart of the poem.

1.1.4.meaning: Khayzala: a slow, loose, swaying walk, said of women.

1.2.4.meaning: Haydhaba (also haydaba): a fast, purposeful pace of camels; some say of horses.

2.1.3.head: بُجاوِيّة
2.1.3.meaning: Bajawi: from Bajawa, a Berber tribe in al-Wahidi, a land in Nubia in al-Barquqi, whose camels were known for speed.

2.2.1.head: خَنوف
2.2.1.meaning: Khanuf: a camel that throws her forefeet outwards as she goes, a sign of spirit.

4.1.3.head: التّيه
4.1.3.meaning: Al-Tih: “the wilderness”, here the Wilderness of the Israelites in Sinai, between al-Qulzum (Suez) and Ayla, which he crossed in his flight.

6.1.2.head: نَخل
6.1.2.meaning: Nakhl: a known watering place on his route.

7.1.3.head: النِّقاب
7.1.3.meaning: Al-Naqab: a place where the road forks; the word runs over into the second half.

7.2.4-5.head: وادي القُرى
7.2.4-5.meaning: Wadi al-Qura: “the valley of villages”, between Medina and Syria.

8.2.3.head: تُربان
8.2.3.meaning: Turban: a place on his route; Ibn Jinni puts it in Iraq, Ibn al-Iflili far from it.

9.1.2.head: حِسمى
9.1.2.meaning: Hisma: a desert place with water; al-Ukbari says the poet called it the most pleasant land on earth.

9.1.4.head: الدَّبور
9.1.4.meaning: Dabur: the west wind. The word runs over into the second half.

11.1.2.head: بُسَيطَة
11.1.2.meaning: Busayta: open desert on the way to Kufa. Here, al-Wahidi says, one of the poet's slaves took a wild bull for a minaret and another an ostrich for a palm tree.

11.1.4.head: الرِّداء
11.1.4.meaning: Rida': a cloak worn over the shoulders. The word runs over into the second half.

13.2.2.head: الشَّغور
13.2.2.meaning: Al-Shughur: a place on the edge of Iraq; the Arabs said, “Whoever reaches al-Shughur has entered Iraq.”

14.1.3.head: الدِّئداء
14.1.3.meaning: Di'da': a pace faster than a trot.

15.2.4.meaning: Suwa: piles of stones set up along a desert road to mark the way.

16.1.4.head: الجَوز
16.1.4.meaning: Jawz: the middle of something; the middle of the night.

17.1.4.head: الرِّماح
17.1.4.meaning: Spears. The word runs over into the second half.

19.2.2.head: العَواصِم
19.2.2.meaning: Al-Awasim: “the strongholds”, the frontier lands of northern Syria around Antioch, in Sayf al-Dawla's realm.

23.2.5.meaning: Tawa: ruin, perishing; first said of lost wealth.

25.1.2.head: الخُوَيدِم
25.1.2.meaning: Khuwaydim: “little servant”, a contemptuous diminutive for Kafur; people called a eunuch a “servant”.
